66009.etyen: Borrowed from Middle Low German untūch, formed from un- (“un-, not”) and tǖch (“stuff, gear, equipment”). a male given name from Arabic
a surname from Arabic, ultimately from the male given name Mohammad

1001177.etyen:
Borrowed from Arabic مُحَمَّد (muḥammad, “praised, commendable”), through a Latin-script transliteration of the Arabic name. The Arabic form is the passive participle of Arabic حَمَّدَ (ḥammada, “to praise, commend”), from the root ح م د (ḥ-m-d, “praise”).
Related Arabic names include أَحْمَد (ʔaḥmad, “more praiseworthy”) and مَحْمُود (maḥmūd, “praised”).

en.g: sharp (♯); appended to a note name to form the name of the note a semitone higher
x: Tonen f hevet et halvt tonetrinn kalles fiss.
The note F raised by one semitone is called F-sharp.

1001945.etyen:
Borrowed from German -is (“sharp-note-forming suffix”). The further origin is uncertain; the German suffix is possibly a shortening of Diesis (“diesis”), from Latin diesis (“musical interval”), from Ancient Greek δίεσις (díesis, “passing through; interval”), a derivative of διΐημι (diḯēmi, “to send or pass through”), itself formed from διά (diá, “through, across”) + ἵημι (híēmi, “to send, let go”). The latter is from Proto-Hellenic *yīyēmi, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- (“to throw”).
Compare the parallel borrowings Finnish -is and Icelandic -ís (“sharp-note-forming suffix”).

The word is used in a specific, well-known sketch making fun of the Danish language from a Norwegian perspective, portraying it as difficult to understand, so much so that Danish people are not even able to understand each other. 1005017.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian frendkona (“kinswoman, female relative”), from Old Norse frændkona (“kinswoman, female relative”), itself formed from frændi (“kinsman, relative”) and kona (“woman, wife”), literally “kinsman-woman”.
The first element frændi is from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (“friend, loved one”), originally the present participle of Proto-Germanic *frijōną (“to love”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preyH- (“to please; love”). The second element kona is from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”).
